extractions.extraction_text: progressive stiffness and pain in the lower back with intermittent cramps over a 3-year period; cramps were extremely painful; sensitivity to any sudden movement or external stimulation; lower back stiffness causing great difficulty performing daily activities and walking with a rigid and straight back; stiffness of the muscles subsided during normal sleep; left L5 radiculopathy
Electromyography showed spontaneous continuous muscle fiber activity which was markedly suppressed after a trial with 20 mg intravenous diazepam
progressive stiffness and pain in the lower back of 3 years' duration
electromyograms showed continuous muscle fiber activity that responded dramatically to diazepam and fulfilled the diagnosis of SMS
treatment with oral diazepam 80 mg daily, tapered to 15 mg daily
muscular stiffness disappeared during treatment with oral diazepam without any recurrence of spasm for 20 months

rigidity and pain in the lower back persisted and even progressed to the upper back and neck; limbs gradually affected with more severe symptoms proximally located; intermittent cramps easily induced by sudden movements or unexpected noise; walked slowly with a stiff spine and limbs; inability to bend waist; great difficulty performing daily activities, particularly putting on shoes and trousers; unable to drive a car due to limited neck mobility; muscular stiffness and pain subsided during normal sleep; speech was normal
myelography and computed tomography of the whole spine showed a laterally protruding disc in the L5-S1 intervertebral space with compression of the left S1 root
received discectomy with subsequent medical and rehabilitation treatment; previous drug treatment included indomethacin, mefenamic acid, tolmetin, acetaminophen, baclofen, and fludiazepam
No history of trauma or infection was noted, and no family members had neurologic disorders

extremestiffness and intermittent cramps in the paraspinal muscles of the whole back and in the proximal limbs with profuse sweating; severe cramp induced by unexpected tap or sudden stretch of the limbs; able to walk a few steps slowly then required support; neck and back flexion limited

attributes.tendon_reflexes: normal except absence of ankle jerk on the left side
attributes.muscle_atrophy: mild atrophy of the left calf muscle
attributes.sensory: mildly decreased pin-prick sensation in the posterior surface of the left lower leg and plantar area due to S1 root compression

extractions.extraction_text: S1 root compression causing sensory deficit

Electromyographic studies from thoracic spinal muscles showed spontaneous muscle fiber activity at rest; continued muscle fiber activity for 20 minutes after 200 mg of intravenous phenytoin; dramatic suppression of muscle fiber activity 20 minutes after 20 mg of intravenous diazepam; abolition of muscle fiber activity 5 minutes after secobarbital-induced sleep

Laboratory examination included hemogram, fasting glucose, liver and renal function tests, electrolytes, creatine phosphokinase, antinuclear antibody, LE cell, rheumatoid factor, complement (3 and 4), HLA B27, immunoglobulins, protein electrophoresis, immunoelectrophoresis, anti-DNA antibody, antimitochondrial antibody, antimicrosomal antibody, thyroid function tests, cortisol, carcinoembryonic antigen, and cerebrospinal fluid studies; all results were within normal limits
Nerve conduction velocities, evoked potentials and electroencephalography were also normal

axial and proximal stiffness starting from the lower back with progressive involvement of the neck and limbs; stiffness very sensitive to external stimulation, particularly sudden movement, frequently inducing painful cramp
EMG investigation revealed continuous muscle activity dramatically suppressed in response to high-dose diazepam
oral diazepam therapy (initial dose 15 mg/day; maintenance dose 80 mg/day for 6 months); dosage tapered to 15 mg daily in the following 20-month period

muscular stiffness and cramps disappeared within one month; no drowsiness, weakness or respiratory suppression during diazepam therapy; patient was well and went back to work 6 months later; stiffness and pain did not recur
The pathogenesis in the present patient appear to be idiopathic, as there was no association with diabetes mellitus, other autoimmune diseases or malignancy
